one_liner: Keyed CLMUL-based C string hash with a proven almost-universal collision bound; 1.5-2.5x CityHash64 bulk throughput, roughly xxh3 parity.
what_it_does: UMASH is a keyed 64-bit string hash plus an optional 128-bit fingerprint (two independent 64-bit hashes computed in one pass), shipped as umash.c/umash.h with an optional umash_long.inc for long inputs. You first build a 304-byte struct umash_params, either from random bytes via umash_params_prepare or deterministically from a 64-bit value and a 32-byte secret via umash_params_derive. You then call umash_full (hash) or umash_fprint (fingerprint), or use the incremental umash_init / umash_sink_update / umash_digest API, which returns the same value as the one-shot call. It is not a drop-in for CityHash64 or xxh3: the signature, the mandatory parameter struct and the output values all differ.
how_it_is_fast: It follows the UMAC/VHASH two-level design. 256-byte blocks are compressed by an 'OH' function that is mostly PH, a carry-less analogue of NH (XOR each 16-byte chunk with key words, then one PCLMULQDQ/PMULL per chunk). The last chunk goes through ENH, a 64x64->128 integer multiply. Block outputs feed a Horner polynomial hash modulo 2^61-1 with lazy reduction. Inputs of 8 bytes or less take a SplitMix64-style mixer, and inputs of 9-16 bytes take a single ENH multiply. From 1 KiB up, umash_long.inc switches to an AVX2 + VPCLMULQDQ routine picked at runtime through CPUID.
when_to_use: Hash tables, sharding or sampling keyed with random per-process params, where you want a stated worst-case collision bound (below ceil(s/4096)*2^-55 for inputs of s bytes or fewer) instead of an empirical SMHasher pass

Content fingerprinting or dedup that needs 128-bit fingerprints with a collision bound below 2^-70 for inputs up to 5 GiB, made reproducible across runs with umash_params_derive and a per-program secret
Replacing CityHash64 in C on x86-64 with CLMUL or aarch64 with the crypto extension: 1.5-2.5x its bulk throughput in rurban SMHasher and slightly fewer cycles per small key
Streaming or chunked inputs: the sink API gives the same value as a one-shot hash, and a sink can be byte-copied to snapshot its state
Long buffers (1 KiB and up) on CPUs that report VPCLMULQDQ, where the AVX2 path gives the README's 10.9 bytes/cycle (39.5 GiB/s) on an EPYC 7713
when_not_to_use: Latency-bound small keys: rurban SMHasher shows about 41 cycles per 1-31 byte key against about 29 for xxh3 and wyhash and 22 for rapidhash on the Ryzen 5 3350G table
When you only want the most bulk throughput: it trails xxh3 by 12% on EPYC 9554P and 31% on i7-6820HQ, and the AES-based gxhash and lanehash rows are more than 2x faster
MSVC, big-endian, 32-bit targets, or CPUs without CLMUL/PMULL: umash.c stops with #error on an unsupported platform, and the README says only gcc-compatible compilers work

Adversaries who can learn or infer the params: the header says the bounds then no longer apply. It is not a MAC or PRF, and umash_params_derive with a NULL key uses the public default secret 'Do not use UMASH VS adversaries.'
Hash values persisted across library versions when params come from umash_params_prepare: the README says the ABI is not final and the same random bytes may produce different params later

integration.dependencies: none (Salsa20 for umash_params_derive is built in; systemtap sdt.h only if UMASH_STAP_PROBE is set)
integration.min_toolchain: gcc-compatible C compiler with GCC 5-era integer-overflow builtins and __uint128_t; C11 <stdatomic.h> for x86-64 dynamic dispatch; inline asm used on GCC 6+ / clang 10+ (optional). MSVC not supported
integration.platforms: x86-64 with CLMUL (-mpclmul), plus a runtime-dispatched AVX2+VPCLMULQDQ path for inputs of 1 KiB or more; little-endian aarch64 with crypto extension (-march=armv8-a+crypto)
integration.thread_safety: One-shot umash_full/umash_fprint only read a caller-owned const umash_params, and the lazily set dispatch pointer is a C11 atomic. Sharing a umash_state across threads is not documented; treat each state as single-owner.

gotchas: The seed argument changes the output but carries no collision bound. Only randomly generated, secret umash_params give the guarantee.
umash_full(..., which=1) computes a full fingerprint and returns its second half, so it is as slow as umash_fprint.

The proof has a known gap. Open issue #40 (Sept 2026) shows the whitepaper's 'reduce mod 2^61-1 loses ~6 bits' step does not follow as written. Third-party paper proofs, only partly Lean-checked, restore the headline 64-bit and 128-bit bounds in an ideal full-key model that does not cover Salsa20-derived params. The maintainer acknowledged this and a doc update is pending.

The Python reference (umash_reference.py) uses one polynomial multiplier for both fingerprint halves, and issue #40 shows its fingerprint does not meet the 2^-83 bound. The C library uses two independent multipliers and is not affected.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick UMASH over xxHash (xxh3), wyhash and rapidhash when a provable almost-universal bound or a 128-bit fingerprint with a stated collision probability matters more than small-key latency. Against CLHash, the other CLMUL almost-universal hash in the catalog, UMASH's case rests on its aarch64 PMULL port, incremental API and fingerprint mode.
verified_claims_summary: In rurban/smhasher's 256 KiB bulk test (CMake Release, -march=native, compiler unstated), umash64 did 21,964 MiB/s vs City64 14,390 on a Ryzen 5 3350G (about 1.5x), 40,087 vs 15,791 on an EPYC 9554P (2.5x) and 30,586 vs 16,062 on an i7-6820HQ (1.9x). Against xxh3 it is +5% on the 3350G and 12% and 31% slower on the other two. The README's headline 26,628 vs 20,854 MiB/s row compares runs converted at different clock rates, so it overstates the gap.
status_note: Active but low-churn: the algorithm has been frozen since 2022 and 2025-2026 commits are warning fixes, formatting and test-dependency updates (last 2026-01-11). It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor (two C files plus an optional .inc), and a thin Rust wrapper, umash-rs, exists (2 stars, last push 2025-01).
